heading: Beyond color: see what the eye sees.
screen_intro: Mix a little light. See how your eye responds. Explore how three kinds of cone cells help us experience a world of color.
pigments_intro: Choose a pigment. Explore the light it reflects and how that spectrum stimulates the S, M and L cones.
footer: A SMALL LAB FOR A COLORFUL WORLD
sensitivity_heading: What each cone is sensitive to
eye_caption: Light reaches the cone cells in your retina.
pigment_swatch_description: sRGB preview of the pigment under the selected incident light
pigment_model_limits: Indigo uses reflectance digitized from a published measurement of indigo-dyed cotton. It represents a dark fabric blue, not pure pigment or every denim wash. Anthocyanin, chlorophyll and carotenoids use published absorption shapes to model a non-scattering layer over a perfect white backing: light crosses the layer twice, giving R = 10⁻²ᴬ. One-way peak absorbance is set to 1 as a chosen layer strength. This is not measured reflectance of pure molecules or a complete leaf or paint model. Concentration, solvent, pH, substrate and scattering affect real colors; the square is an sRGB approximation.
pigment_model_spectrum: Anthocyanin, chlorophyll and carotenoids use the solid PROSPECT-D curves in Féret et al. (2017), Figure 8, manually digitized from 400 to 750 nm at 10 nm intervals with extra points at sharp features. Dashed curves and shaded bands are excluded. The 400 nm endpoints are held to 390 nm; the zero 750 nm endpoints are held to 780 nm. These tails are assumptions. Each absorption shape is scaled to peak one-way absorbance 1. Indigo uses the sample No. 1 cotton reflectance in Kawahito & Yasukawa (2009), Figure 3a, approximately digitized every 10 nm from 400 to 700 nm, with constant endpoint extensions to 390 and 780 nm and no peak scaling. Samples are linearly interpolated to 1 nm. CIE and D65 tables are from Colour Science v0.4.6.
outgoing_caption:
Dashed: incident light E.
Solid: reflected light E × R.
preview_caption: Approximate sRGB appearance under the selected light. No eye adaptation is simulated; warm light retains its warm cast.
response_caption: 100% is a perfect white reflector under the selected light, separately for each cone. These are relative excitations, not firing rates.
math_grid: 1. Align the wavelengths. Join neighboring samples with straight lines to evaluate all tables from 390 to 780 nm in 1 nm steps.
math_reflectance: 2. Find reflectance R. Indigo supplies measured-reflectance samples; lighter indigo is five times the original indigo reflectance, with no white component. Absorbance inputs transmit 10⁻ᴬ per pass. Two passes through a layer over white backing give R = 10⁻²ᴬ. For example, A = 1 gives R = 0.01 (1%).
math_light: 3. Calculate the light reaching the eye: L(λ) = E(λ) × R(λ), where E is the selected incident spectrum. All sources are scaled to the same ∫ E ȳ dλ (white-reflector luminance). Reflectance describes the material; L describes the outgoing light.
math_cones: 4. Weight that light by each cone sensitivity C. Response (%) = 100 × ∫ E R C dλ / ∫ E C dλ. The denominator is that cone’s response to white. A flat R = 0.5 gives 50% for all three cones.
math_integral: The integral means area under a curve. Numerically, add trapezoids: ∫ f dλ ≈ Σ (λᵢ₊₁ − λᵢ) × (fᵢ + fᵢ₊₁) / 2. Each interval here is 1 nm.
math_rgb: 5. Calculate the preview separately. Integrate outgoing light against CIE x̄, ȳ, z̄ and divide by ∫ E ȳ dλ, giving white Y = 1 under the selected lamp. Convert XYZ to linear sRGB for a D65 display, clip to 0–1, then encode and multiply by 255. No chromatic adaptation is applied: a white reflector may look warm or tinted. The S/M/L bars are not RGB channels.
light_white_note: Ideal equal-energy white: constant spectral power per nanometer, not an RGB screen spectrum.
light_d65_note: CIE D65 reference daylight, interpolated from the bundled 5 nm table.
light_incandescent_note: Illustrative incandescent bulb: a 2856 K blackbody from Planck’s law. Real tungsten bulbs differ with temperature and emissivity.
denim_explanation: The original indigo curve is already a dark dyed-cotton sample, not pure indigo dye. Its measured reflectance is only about 2.5–8%. Denim often combines indigo-dyed warp yarns with undyed filling yarns. Indigo ring dyeing leaves pale yarn cores; wear and finishing remove surface color and reveal more of that pale cotton. Dye loading and fabric construction also vary, so one dark sample cannot represent every pair of jeans.
denim_model: The lighter example uses R_light = 5 × R_dark, with no added white component. Its reflectance spans 12.5–40%, so no spectral clipping is needed. Multiplication preserves the spectral shape and chromaticity before display gamut clipping, while making the reflected light five times stronger. This is a brightness-scaling illustration, not a measured jeans spectrum or a model of dye concentration or wear.
denim_reference: CottonWorks: denim construction and ring dyeing
light_tube_note: CIE FL2 fluorescent-tube reference: phosphor emission together with mercury-vapor lines. Represents a typical tube spectrum, not every fluorescent lamp. CIE 2018 data, CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped to 390–780 nm and scaled to equal white-reflector luminance.
spectrum_caption: Three hypothetical RGB emitters. The dark line is their sum; your screen’s spectrum will differ.
model_summary: About the model and its limits
model_conversion: We decode sRGB to linear light, multiply by luminosity (a relative intensity control), then convert through CIE XYZ to approximate Hunt–Pointer–Estevez S, M and L responses. Each cone is normalized to its response to full-intensity sRGB white (100%). These are relative excitations, not measured firing rates or percentages of cone cells activated. The displayed square is re-encoded to sRGB after dimming.
model_limits: RGB does not specify a unique spectrum. This illustration assumes an ideal sRGB display and does not model adaptation, rods, individual differences or your screen’s calibration. Luminosity here is not an absolute physical unit.
model_spectrum: The spectrum is an illustrative sum of Gaussian RGB emission bands centered at 625, 535 and 460 nm (widths σ = 18, 22 and 16 nm). Their amplitudes follow linear-light RGB and luminosity on a fixed scale. It is not a measured spectrum or an exact spectral match to sRGB. The sensitivity panel shows peak-normalized Stockman–Sharpe 2° energy fundamentals. These two panels explain emission and sensitivity; the response bars continue to use the sRGB-to-Hunt–Pointer–Estevez model described above, rather than integrating the illustrative spectrum.
